title: Format Traps: Points-League Players and 9-Cat Fluff
brief: Which players are likely mispriced in our room because their value comes from points-league scoring or from inflated 9-cat totals, and which are undervalued for a category league? Tiers must separate players to avoid at market price from players to target.
summary: Our Yahoo room mixes points-league and category pricing. That inflates high-usage scorers like Cade Cunningham, Jalen Johnson, Jalen Brunson, Josh Giddey and Alperen Sengun, plus "9-cat fluff" players whose season totals or z-scores look better than their weekly H2H value. Let others pay those prices. Spend the savings on cheap category profiles such as Jaren Jackson Jr., Dyson Daniels, Nickeil Alexander-Walker, Paul George, OG Anunoby and Derrick White.

sections.heading: Why our room misprices by format

paragraphs.text: Yahoo ADP mixes owners drafting for points with owners drafting for categories. So points-league favorites show up high in category rooms and at the top of autodraft queues. Our auction runs on Yahoo, so expect Yahoo average costs to carry some points-league bias. When a player has a big gap between his points value and his category value, the price is often wrong for us. Buy when the room prices him for the other format.

The usual points-league trap is a high-usage scorer. Volume points count fully in Yahoo points scoring. In our 9-cat H2H league, efficiency, assists, steals and blocks matter more, and turnovers count against you. A scorer with few other strengths can be top 10 in points leagues and only a third-rounder in categories. Before you bid, compare each player's points tag and category tag in our notes. If the Yahoo cost is above the category cap the experts give, drop out at that cap.

sections.heading: Points-league scorers to let go at market price

paragraphs.text: Cade Cunningham is the biggest early trap. He could finish ahead of Shai in points leagues but sits around 6th to 10th in categories. His turnovers cost the most, and his FG% and FT% are only middling for a first-rounder. The experts cap him at about 45 to 50 USD, well below his Yahoo cost. Jalen Johnson is the same story one round later. He is priced as a first-rounder but graded round two in 9-cat, so stop at about 35 to 40 USD.

In the middle rounds, Jalen Brunson's value is mostly points, assists and FT%, with almost no rebounds, steals or blocks. Category experts put him near 18 to 20 USD, so let someone else pay 30 USD or more. Josh Giddey is graded around picks 11 to 15 in points leagues against 20 to 25 in categories, so 28 to 32 USD is the limit. Alperen Sengun rates higher in points leagues than in 9-cat. Do not follow the market above about 30 USD. Pascal Siakam is a points-league top 30 but only 50 to 60 in categories. Pay his Yahoo level, not ESPN's or last season's 25 USD.

Late in the draft the same rule covers Stephon Castle (top 50 in points, around 80 in categories, so bid single digits), AJ Dybantsa (a volume scorer every expert says to avoid in the top 100, 1 USD only) and Ja Morant (about 5 USD, 10 USD at most). RJ Barrett and Jonathan Kuminga are scoring-only profiles with FT% damage. Treat both as 1 USD flyers at most.

sections.heading: Nine-cat fluff: totals that overstate H2H value

paragraphs.text: Some players look better in standard 9-cat rankings than they really are. One expert calls them nine-cat fluffies: the turnover-inclusive z-score method lifts them. Another warns that fluffed players get overdrafted. For us, the test is weekly H2H value, not season totals.

Mikal Bridges is the clearest case. Games played inflate his totals, and ESPN ranks him 29th, but every expert puts him near pick 98, or about 2 USD. Reed Sheppard was about 30th in season-total 9-cat last season but 93rd in H2H, so spend 1 to 3 USD at most. Chet Holmgren's blocks inflate his z-score rank. Do not pay more than about 21 to 22 USD.

The cheap centers carry the same tag. Jarrett Allen is lifted by turnover-inclusive z-scores, so 8 to 12 USD is fair and his ESPN rank of 51 is not. Ivica Zubac's past rank of 35 overstated him, so aim for 10 to 14 USD and let someone else pay 20. Josh Hart's value comes from FG% on low volume, so pay 2 to 3 USD. Cason Wallace's steals inflate his rank, so he is a 1 USD steals source. Do not pay the 8 USD seen in mocks.

The reverse gap is where we gain value. Jaren Jackson Jr. ranks about 36th in categories, and his ADP leans toward his points value. That puts his average cost well below his Yahoo value, so he is a buy anywhere near market. Dyson Daniels is a steals specialist that experts value at 20 USD or more, so anything under that is a buy. Nickeil Alexander-Walker's points-league value matches his ADP, but he is a top 40 to 50 category player. Target him near 15 to 20 USD.

Defense and shooting profiles with no weak category are also cheap. Paul George is worth more in 9-cat than in points, so 10 to 15 USD is good value. OG Anunoby is much worse in points leagues, and experts value him near 20 USD in categories. Derrick White is a 3PM, AST and guard-BLK source to target at his Yahoo range, not at ESPN's value. Naz Reid goes earlier in category leagues, so 10 to 14 USD is fair. Jaden McDaniels (steals and blocks) and Ty Jerome (3PM, AST, STL, FT%) are top-100 category players at Yahoo prices near the bottom of the draft.

In the early rounds, Giannis Antetokounmpo is the case where plain 9-cat and roto ranks undersell an H2H player. His FT% drag lowers those ranks, but experts treat him as a clear number 5 pick in H2H categories. Plan for about 60 USD and a punt FT% build. LaMelo Ball is second round in categories and third round in points, so anything near 30 USD is fair. Amen Thompson is tier five in points but round two to three in cats. At 35 to 38 USD he is fair while he slides.

The tags do not always point one way. Paolo Banchero is tagged as a points-league player, but he was about 125th in nine-cat and 58th in head-to-head last season. The points side says his ADP in the 30s is inflated. The H2H side says his Yahoo rank of 51 is fair. Pay around 19 to 20 USD. Jaylen Brown has both tags too. He is about 10th in points against about 25th in categories, so pay the 20 to 24 USD category price, not last season's 29 USD. The fluff tag does not always mean avoid, either. Kel'el Ware, Day'Ron Sharpe and Onyeka Okongwu are tagged fluff but trade far below their site values. They stay buys at up to 10 USD, 5 to 8 USD and the low teens.

The experts also split on some category-player prices. On Kevin Durant, most see a late first-rounder and expect 40 to 46 USD in our room, but Josh found 40 USD too rich. On Paul George, most call 10 to 15 USD good value, while Josh would go up to 20 USD. On Lauri Markkanen, the experts' round-3 grade fits the mid-20s, but one mock already reached 30 USD. In each case, set your cap at the lower expert number. Only go past it if the player fills a build need.

Before the 2026-10-18 auction, write a cap next to every points-tagged player: Cade 45 to 50, Jalen Johnson 35 to 40, Giddey 32, Sengun 30, Brunson 20. Do the same for the fluff names: Chet 22, Zubac 14, Allen 12, Bridges and Hart 2 to 3, Sheppard and Wallace 1 to 3. Clear Yahoo autodraft queues from your thinking, because they push points-league players up. If a manager in our room drafts on autopilot, those players go early and our targets slide.

After the draft, test the format gap with weekly H2H numbers, not season totals. A points-tagged scorer whose FG% and turnovers sink you each week is a trade chip before the 2027-03-04 deadline. Sell him to a manager who values his raw points. A fluff player whose value is only games played is a drop candidate once waivers offer a starter with real minutes.
